title: Storytelling: Story-Driven Explanations That Build Schema and Boost Learning [FREE RESOURCE]
author: Jamie Lee Clark
summary: Jamie Lee Clark's DistillED newsletter makes the case for story-driven explanation as a way to build schema and make content memorable. Drawing on Daniel Willingham's claim that memory depends on what students think about, he argues that stories direct attention to meaning because students hunt for cause-and-effect links and want to know what happens next. He offers Ros Atkins's story structures (chronological, finish-start-finish, zoom out, what someone said) as planning tools, and Willingham's Four Cs of causality, conflict, complications and character as organising principles rather than a rigid sequence. A Henry VIII example, a planning template and a CPD slideshow sit behind the paid tier, so the free text is a compact overview of the argument.
points: Stories help because students look for causal links and care about the outcome, so they think about meaning rather than disconnected facts.
Willingham's Four Cs (causality, conflict, complications, character) work as planning principles across lessons, not a fixed sequence.
Ros Atkins's structures such as finish-start-finish and zoom out give teachers concrete ways to shape an explanation.
A senior colleague's pressure-cooker framing of the ranch in Of Mice and Men shows how a well-delivered narrative frame can organise a whole text.
quotes: In the classroom, storytelling helps explain concepts and important ideas in ways that make content more interesting, memorable, and easier to understand. When I was an NQT (newly qualified teacher), I remember a senior colleague describing the ranch in Of Mice and Men as a pressure cooker.

Journalist and author Ros Atkins also highlights how powerful narrative can be: when we shape information as a structured story—with a clear purpose, tension, and progression—it becomes far more engaging and easier for students to follow and remember.

Daniel Willingham explains that the most important factor in memory is what students think about while learning. Stories help focus that thinking on meaning, because they naturally encourage students to look for connections, grapple with questions, and care about what happens next.

The human mind seems exquisitely tuned to understand and remember stories -so much so that psychologists sometimes refer to stories as ‘psychologically privileged,’ meaning that they are treated differently in memory than other types of material.

Willingham argues that structuring lessons with the Four Cs—causality, conflict, complications, and character—and ensuring students understand the central question helps them think about the meaning of what they are learning, rather than just memorising disconnected facts.
